channel.title: Brutus on Anti-Federalist Library
channel.description: Recent content in Brutus on Anti-Federalist Library

item.title: Brutus I
item.description: Argues that the proposed Constitution would create a consolidated national government, threatening individual liberties and state sovereignty.

item.title: Brutus II
item.description: Emphasizes the necessity of a Bill of Rights to safeguard individual freedoms against potential federal overreach.

item.title: Brutus III
item.description: Criticizes the apportionment of representation in Congress, asserting it disadvantages smaller states and lacks true proportionality.

item.title: Brutus IV
item.description: Expresses concern that the small size of the House of Representatives would lead to an elite ruling class detached from the populace.

item.title: Brutus IX
item.description: Advocates for clear limitations on governmental powers to prevent the erosion of individual rights and freedoms.

item.title: Brutus V
item.description: Warns that the Necessary and Proper Clause grants Congress expansive powers that could undermine state authority.

item.title: Brutus VI
item.description: Highlights the dangers of federal taxation powers potentially rendering state governments financially dependent and powerless.

item.title: Brutus VII
item.description: Continues the discussion on taxation, arguing that concurrent taxation powers would lead to conflicts detrimental to state functions.

item.title: Brutus VIII
item.description: Opposes the maintenance of a standing army in peacetime, fearing it could be used to suppress civil liberties.

item.title: Brutus X
item.description: Draws from historical examples to illustrate how standing armies have historically led to the downfall of free governments.

item.title: Brutus XI
item.description: Raises concerns about the federal judiciary’s potential to expand its power beyond constitutional limits.

item.title: Brutus XII
item.description: Argues that the federal courts would gradually encroach upon and diminish state judicial authority.

item.title: Brutus XIII
item.description: Questions the propriety of allowing individuals to sue states in federal courts, fearing it undermines state sovereignty.

item.title: Brutus XIV
item.description: Critiques the appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court, suggesting it could overwhelm state courts and laws.

item.title: Brutus XV
item.description: Warns that the Supreme Court’s interpretative powers could effectively allow it to shape the Constitution to its will.

item.title: Brutus XV
item.description: Examines the Senate’s structure and powers, expressing concern over its potential to dominate the legislative process.
